title: Changing team meetings to repair a working relationship
subtitle: When one working relationship kept breaking down, I changed how the team worked instead of trying to change the person. The new habits became everyone's.

card.title: Repairing a team dynamic through process
card.line: I changed how the team worked instead of the person, and the new habits spread.

team: Team of five, including a design lead

sections.headline: Changing team meetings to repair a working relationship
sections.subtext: As Head of Product Design at a B2B platform company, I led a team of five and had a design function to build. The lesson I use most came from somewhere else: a working relationship that kept breaking down, and what changed when I stopped looking at the person and started looking at the conditions.

sections.headline: Change the conditions, and the collaboration follows

metrics.label: The setting
metrics.value: A B2B platform company in the middle of a platform shift. I was Head of Product Design, leading a team of five, including a design lead.

metrics.label: The problem
metrics.value: One engineer's work wasn't landing with the team. Meetings were tense, points got cut off, and the team had learned to route around the collaboration.

metrics.label: What changed
metrics.value: I changed the conditions the team met under: agendas shared early, material sent ahead, turn-taking on purpose, decisions in writing. Within months the dynamic shifted, and the habits became the team's default. What I observed as the team's lead; nothing here was measured.

metrics.label: Three takeaways
metrics.value: Ask what's wrong with the system before you ask what's wrong with the person. Make the cheap conditions the default. Answer "why change for one person?" with the cost.

sections.headline: Quick syncs that ran for an hour
sections.content:
The meetings had a pattern. A "quick sync" turned into an hour-long debate nobody could have prepared for. No agenda went out in advance. Discussion was fast and verbal, and whoever spoke first and loudest set the direction.

One engineer's points got cut off before they were finished. The discussion moved on. Over time, the team learned to route around the collaboration rather than work through it.

sections.headline: When collaboration fails, the reflex is to manage the person
sections.content:
This is a story about that working relationship, and about the question I ended up asking instead of the usual one.

The usual one is about the individual: what is wrong with that person? It is the comfortable question, because the answer never involves your own process. The question I now ask first is about the system, and it travels to almost any team.

sections.headline: Excellent work that kept getting talked over
sections.content:
I had joined to make design a real function, with the same weight as product and engineering. I built a planning process so design, product and engineering worked from the same picture. The design system was mine, and I set up joint governance with engineering around it.

Inside that team, one collaboration kept failing. It did not add up. The engineering work itself was excellent, and the ideas, once there was room for them, were often the sharpest in the room. They just kept getting talked over.

sections.headline: I stopped assessing a person and started recording conditions
sections.content:
So I started watching the pattern instead of the person. When did this collaboration fail, and when did it work?

It failed in fast, talk-over-each-other discussion and under time pressure. It worked in writing, and with time to think before answering.

Our collaboration ran on one default: fast, verbal, loudest voice first. It filtered out good ideas before anyone heard them.

images.alt: Two-part diagram. Above, the order input arrived in: fastest to speak, loudest to hold the floor, whoever remembered it after, then the decision — with no agenda, no prep time and nothing written down. Below, three boxes: the discussion, an engineer, the decision. The link into the engineer is marked cut off and the link out is marked rarely arrived, and a dashed arc runs beneath from the discussion straight to the decision, bypassing them.
images.caption: The pattern I was actually looking at, once I stopped looking at the person.

sections.headline: Five changes to how the team worked, none of them about one person
sections.content: Every one of these changed the conditions the whole team worked under. All of them were cheap, and all of them applied to everybody.

steps.label: Agendas, shared early
steps.description: Every meeting got a written agenda in advance. No more "quick syncs" that turned into hour-long debates no one could prepare for.

steps.label: Room to prepare
steps.description: Context and material went out before group discussions, so thinking could happen ahead of the meeting rather than under time pressure inside it.

steps.label: Turn-taking, on purpose
steps.description: In group settings I made space for sequential input, instead of letting whoever spoke loudest set the outcome.

steps.label: Decisions in writing
steps.description: Important decisions were written down, so nobody had to rely on their own memory of the conversation.

steps.label: Coaching the design lead
steps.description: I coached my design lead through the same shift: how to work through a strained engineering relationship directly, rather than routing around it.

images.alt: Five changed conditions across a band — agendas shared early, room to prepare, turn-taking on purpose, decisions in writing, coaching the design lead — and beneath each, the property it puts back: thinking time, processing before rather than under pressure, sequence instead of volume, one record instead of five recollections, and the same shift one level down.
images.caption: Five changes to how the team worked. None of them about anyone in particular.

sections.headline: "Why change for one person?" Because the process had a cost.
sections.content:
Not everyone agreed. "Why should we change how we work for one person?" came sometimes out loud, sometimes through eye-rolls and foot-dragging.

Part of my answer was about fairness. Equality is everyone getting the same thing. Equity is everyone getting what they need to contribute, and people need different conditions to do their best work.

The other part was the plain business case. Our process was filtering out good ideas before they were heard. That is a cost, on top of the fairness question.

sections.headline: Within months, the habits belonged to everyone

metrics.label: The collaboration
metrics.before: Tension, points dismissed, the team routing around the working relationship
metrics.after: Ideas got airtime, and problems others missed got caught

metrics.label: Team norms
metrics.after: Written agendas, prep time, and documented decisions became how the team worked by default

metrics.label: How the team thought about friction
metrics.value: People started asking what was wrong with the process before deciding what was wrong with a person

sections.narrative:
Within months the dynamic shifted. The bigger change was that the structured habits spread: other people adopted the prep, the agendas and the written decisions for themselves. They stopped being a fix for one situation and became the norm.

None of this was measured. It is what I saw as the team's lead.

sections.headline: The agenda goes out first now
sections.content:
The meetings still happen. The agenda goes out first, the material goes with it, and turns are taken on purpose. A decision ends up in writing instead of in five different memories.

And the points that used to get cut off now get finished.

sections.headline: Three things to try with your own team

steps.label: Ask what's wrong with the system before you ask what's wrong with the person.
steps.description: Write down when a collaboration fails and when it works. If the same person does well in one setting and struggles in another, the setting is your variable.

steps.label: Make the cheap conditions the default.
steps.description: An agenda sent ahead, material before the meeting, turns taken on purpose, the decision in writing. None of it needs a budget, and none of it helps only one person.

steps.label: Answer "why change for one person?" with the cost.
steps.description: Good ideas filtered out before anyone hears them are a business cost. Say so plainly, alongside the fairness argument.

sections.headline: If it fails in every setting, the setting isn't your variable
sections.content: This approach is for collaboration that fails in some conditions and works in others. If it fails everywhere, in writing and with time to prepare too, changing the conditions won't fix it, and you need a different conversation.
Ask me what changed once the agenda started going out in advance, and why habits meant for one working relationship spread to the whole team. Get in touch.

executive.summary: Built a design function as Head of Product Design: a team of five, a design system, a seat at the leadership table. Defining example: diagnosed why one collaboration kept failing, changed how the team worked instead of the person, and the habits became the team's default.
